title: Irena Sendler
hook: a Polish Catholic social worker helps smuggle Jewish children out of the Warsaw Ghetto, and buries their names

segments.voice: Yesterday, Titus Brandsma, carrying the bishops' letter from editor to editor. Your line was a journalist's courage. Did you say your true sentence? Today, a rescuer with a pass and a list. Day nine hundred twelve.

Slips of tissue paper, each with a child's name on it. The real name, the name they were born with, and next to it the new name they now answer to, and where they've been taken. The slips go into glass jars, and the jars go into the ground under an apple tree in a friend's yard in Warsaw. That's the story usually told about Irena Sendler, a Catholic social worker. She buried the names so that one day, when the war was over, someone could dig them up and give the children back their families.
screen: `NAMES ON TISSUE PAPER.` → `JARS UNDER AN APPLE TREE.` → `TO GIVE THE CHILDREN BACK.`

segments.voice: It began with a pass. Irena worked in Warsaw's welfare office. When the Nazis walled the city's Jews into the Ghetto, disease spread inside, and she was able to get a pass to go in as part of the health inspections. Inside, she saw children starving. Second, the network. She was not alone. She worked with a secret Polish group that helped Jews, known by a code name, Żegota, and with others, Catholic and Jewish, inside and outside the walls. Children were carried out in ambulances, in boxes and sacks, through buildings with doors on both sides. Then they needed new names, papers and homes: Polish families, orphanages, convents where sisters took them in. Third, the parents. The hardest moment, by her own later account, was asking Jewish mothers and fathers to hand their children to a stranger, with no promise of anything. Some said yes. Some could not. Fourth, the arrest. The Gestapo arrested her and beat her badly, and she was sentenced to death. Żegota bribed a guard, and she got away and went on working under another name. She never gave up the list. Jesus says in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he that shall receive one such little child in my name, receiveth me." After the war, Israel's Holocaust memorial, Yad Vashem, honored her as Righteous Among the Nations, and in later life she said she had not done enough.
screen: `A PASS INTO THE GHETTO.` · `ŻEGOTA AND THE NETWORK.` · `PARENTS HANDING OVER CHILDREN.` · `ARRESTED, AND STILL THE LIST.` · then, large: `RECEIVE ONE SUCH LITTLE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a rescuer. Settle, and breathe. Hold Irena in mind, and then the people she worked with whose names are less known: the drivers, the sisters, the families who said yes to a child at the door. Let them be real people, with their own fears and their own doors. Then think of someone in your own life who stepped in for someone else when it cost them. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, simply say their name to yourself. The bell holds the time.
